t: Minimum Cuts to Divide a Circle — Case Analysis
o: We must split a circle into n equal slices using straight cuts through the center. Each cut is a diameter line; a cut can serve as a shared boundary for two adjacent slices when cuts are arranged like spokes. Walk the examples: for n = 4, two perpendicular diameters create 4 equal quarters, so 2 cuts suffice. For n = 3, three cuts at 120° apart are needed — with an odd number of slices no two cuts can be collinear (each diameter would produce a pair of opposite slices), so every slice needs its own cut, giving 3. The special case n = 1 needs 0 cuts since the circle is already one piece. With n ≤ 100 the answer is a constant-time formula; constraints imply no simulation or search is needed.
k: n = 1 requires 0 cuts because the circle already consists of exactly one slice.
If n is even, each diameter cut creates two opposite slices, so n/2 cuts suffice.
If n > 1 is odd, no two cuts can share a line (opposite halves would be unequal), so n cuts are required.

a.i: Think about what each cut contributes. A single cut always produces a full diameter, splitting the circle into 2 pieces only if it's the first cut. For even n we can pair slices across the center: each of the n/2 diameters yields two slices, so n/2 cuts work and fewer cannot (each cut adds at most 2 new boundaries). For odd n > 1, slices come in pairs around any diameter, so an odd count forces one unpaired slice per cut — hence n cuts.
s: Else if n is even, return n / 2.
a.t: O(1) — a couple of comparisons on the input.

a.i: The same logic compresses into a single expression. For n = 1 the answer is 0; otherwise the answer is n when n is odd and n/2 when n is even. Note that n - (n % 2) equals n for odd n and n/2... more precisely, the answer for n > 1 is n / 2 + (n % 2) * (n / 2), which simplifies to n * (n % 2 == 0 ? 0.5 : 1). Using integer tricks: answer = (n == 1) ? 0 : (n >> 1) + (n & 1) * (n >> 1), i.e., n/2 doubled when odd — equivalently n & ~((n & 1) ^ 1) adjusted. The cleanest form: return n == 1 ? 0 : (n % 2 ? n : n / 2).
s: Otherwise return n if n is odd, else n / 2, in one expression.

w: In an interview, present Approach 1's reasoning first (why even n allows paired diameters and odd n does not), then land on the one-liner. Common pitfalls: forgetting the n = 1 edge case (returning 1 instead of 0), and assuming the first cut splits the circle for all n — it does not count as producing distinct parts until combined. Follow-ups might ask to generalize to dividing into n equal-area but not necessarily congruent pieces, or to prove optimality formally via counting boundary arcs: k cuts yield at most 2k arc segments, so k ≥ ceil(n/2), with equality achievable only for even n or n = 1.
